paragraphs.text: On the day of the cross, let us offer as our first-fruits a sermon about the cross, and let us crown the day. Or rather, let us be crowned by the memory of the day, for the cross is not crowned by what we say; it is we who receive crowns from it, through what we gratefully confess. Today, brothers, the cross was planted, and the world was sanctified. Today the cross was planted, and death was overthrown. Today the cross shone out, and the demons were scattered. Today the cross won the prize, and the devil was put to shame. Today the cross shone out, and death was conquered, humanity was set free, and God was glorified.

Today, among the Jews, the earth was shaken, but among us the whole world is made firm. Today the God-fighting audacity of the Jews split the rocks; today God-loving piety united the world. It was fitting that the things of piety should be joined together and the things of impiety split apart, as David says: "They were split asunder, yet they were not pierced to the heart." Today, among the Jews, the sun brought on darkness from the sixth hour until the ninth, for the thing made could not bear the outrage done to its Maker. It drew in its rays so as not to become a witness of that God-fighting hatred. It was not that the outrage touched the Godhead; it was that, on the part of those who dared it, what was being done was done as an outrage.

Today, among the Jews, the sun changed its ray; today, among us, grace turns night into day. For piety loves to enjoy light even in darkness, while impiety is filled with darkness even in the light. To the faithful even the night counts as day, but for the unfaithful even the day is turned into night. That is why Scripture, speaking of the faithful, says: "And night is illumination in my delight, for the darkness will not be dark to you, and the night will be bright as the day." So for the believer even night is changed into day, but for the unbeliever even day is turned into night, as the prophet cries out: "They will grope for the wall like the blind, and they will walk at noonday as at midnight."

Today, brothers, Adam was cast out of paradise because of his disobedience; today he is brought back into paradise. And the thief is the witness. A thief went out, and a thief came in: out went the one who stole against the will of the commandment, and in came the one who stole salvation from the cross. I know that I spoke about the thief recently too, but the message of the cross holds many different stories. The one thief is put to death by means of a tree; this thief gathers salvation from a tree like a harvest. Earthly things were not enough for him; he plundered heavenly things too, not cheating by force but winning by faith. For this is the voice of the Master, who says: "The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent take it by force."

On the cross there were two thieves, an image of the Jews and of the Greeks, who at first walked in impiety and afterwards came to know the truth. The thief who remained a thief to the end is an image of the Jews. Up to the cross they ran the road of wickedness together, and the cross divided their roads. For from the cross the two part ways: the road of destruction for those who do not believe, and the road of salvation for those who believe. There the thief learned the difference between the roads, that "the Lord knows the way of the righteous, and the way of the ungodly will perish."

And see God's discernment, so that you too may say with the prophet: "You are righteous, O Lord, and your judgments are upright." For one sin Adam is banished from paradise; for one word of faith the thief is saved. One sin drives Adam out of delight; one act of righteousness settles the thief in delight. The thief entered paradise. O wonder! Not even to Abraham was the promise of paradise given by spoken word. He inherits through faith, but a promise of paradise no one received before the thief.

Pay close attention here, and search the whole of Scripture, Old and New. You will find that none of the righteous before the thief is seen to have received the promise by spoken word: not Abraham, not Moses, not the prophets, not the apostles. Before them all it is the thief who hears: "Truly, truly I say to you, today you will be with me in paradise." God called Abraham, saying: "Go out from your land and from your kindred and from your father's house." He did not say, "so that you may inherit paradise," but, "come into the land that I will show you." God gave Moses the law, and as the fruit of keeping the commandments he promises the good things of the earth: "If you keep the law of the Lord your God." Nowhere is there a promise of paradise before the thief.

We must ask why he made this promise to the thief ahead of the others, ahead of such trustworthy men. Abraham believed God, but he did not believe in God as he appeared in such disgrace. He believed God speaking from heaven; he believed God sending his word through holy angels and delivering his commandment on his own authority. Isaiah believed too, but he had seen him in glory. Ezekiel believed too, but he had beheld him above the cherubim. The prophets believed too, but each of them, in a different way, saw his Master in glory, as far as human nature could see him. Moses believed, but he believed God speaking from the midst of the fire and the thick darkness, the trumpets and the thunders. These things were enough to brace even an unbeliever.

I say this not to belittle the prophets but to speak in defence of the one who received paradise. For he sees the Saviour not on a royal throne, not speaking in the heavens, not giving orders through an angel. He saw him in disgrace and worships him in glory. He saw him on a cross and entreats him as one seated in heaven. He sees him condemned, and he calls the crucified one king, and says: "Remember me when you come into your kingdom."

You see him crucified, and you call one who bears the name of a condemned man a king? You did not read the law, you who spent your time on lawlessness. You did not read the prophets, you who busied yourself with murders. You did not read the divine law while you were sharpening your sword. Where were you taught to think so wisely about Christ? The Jews, who know the law, crucify him; you, who are unacquainted with it, call the condemned man God and worship the crucified one.

Whom did he bring into the glory of the kingdom? We have spoken on behalf of the one who dared, drawing on the events themselves. For we do not imitate the outsiders' art of character-portrayal and personification; we borrow the starting points of our themes from the events themselves. "Who taught you to say such things about him?" "The law did not teach me," he says, "but the sun taught me by hiding itself. I saw it shudder at the outrage of the cross. I saw the earth too split open, unable to bear the Christ-killing beasts. I saw the rocks split as well." The rocks were split, but the ungrateful heart is not broken. The rocks were split, and the curtain of the temple was torn in two.

What is the curtain? It is what we would call a velum, a veil. I have to use this ordinary word, from which everyone understands what the curtain was, not because I am explaining something difficult, but because the term is unintelligible to many. The curtain was a woven fabric made of purple, scarlet, fine linen and blue. So when the cross was being planted, Scripture says, the curtain was torn from top to bottom, the rocks were split, the earth was shaken, the tombs were opened.

The curtain over the double doors is torn, because the king and ruler was no longer in his own house; for the curtain is certainly a sign of authority. After the outrage done to the Most High God, God who dwelt in the temple, and the Holy Spirit, went out of the temple and left the house desolate: "See, your house is left to you desolate." When the King of glory departed, the emblems of the kingdom were torn apart. The tombs burst open. He had not yet gone down to Hades to set things right, and already the earth could not bear the presence of its Master. The rivers burst open, unable to bear the one who had come down to them from above. The tombs burst open and gave up people, who entered the holy city to leave the case settled beyond dispute.

These things happened at the cross, and the Jews mocked him, saying: "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross, and we will believe you." Consider how the voice of the devil's children imitates their father's voice. The devil says to the Saviour on the pinnacle of the temple: "If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down." And the Jews likewise: "If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross, and we will believe you."

They also crucify thieves with him, not because they hated thieves, for they were partners of thieves, but to insult the Master by putting him in the company of thieves, and so that the bystanders would see that he was being judged on a charge of wrongdoing. "Let us crucify with thieves," they say, "the man who has done the same things as thieves." But Isaiah did not keep silent about this staged drama. Seeing the unequal suffering of the righteous one and the unrighteous, he said: "For the sins of the people he came to death, and he was counted among the lawless," that is, among thieves. The Jews did not hate thieves; they wanted to disgrace Christ's passion by the company of thieves.

That they did not hate thieves is clear when Pilate says to them: "Whom shall I release to you, Jesus or Barabbas the robber?" who, Scripture says, had been thrown into prison for murder. And they say: "Release Barabbas to us." The robbers asked for the robber and handed the Lord over to the cross, not overpowering him by force, but handing him over in accordance with the divine plan. Pilate says to them: "Shall I crucify your king?" And they say: "We have no king but Caesar." They denied the kingdom of God and were handed over to the kingdom of the Romans. Because they did not recognize what they had, they received what they asked for.

At the cross they brought thorns as well, and they brought gall too. Foreseeing this, Moses cried out: "Crooked and perverse generation, is this how you repay the Lord?" To the one who gave you manna in the wilderness, do you offer gall? Isaiah, too, rightly says: "I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns." To the one who made good things blossom for you, you offer a crown of thorns. Pilate holds back, and the Jews say: "His blood be on us and on our children."

Let us too say the same words, but not with the same intent: "The blood of Christ be on us and on our children," for them unto condemnation, for us unto righteousness. For the blood of Christ is no weaker than the furnace of Babylon. The furnace of Babylon honoured the saints and consumed the Chaldeans. The precious blood knows how to destroy the unbelieving and to save those who believe.

Light befits the cross, for the cross alone dispelled the darkness of the demons. Were it not for the cross, we would be worshipping demons. The cross pulled down error, the cross made holiness blossom, the cross brought forth the ray of righteousness. Everything we have comes from the cross, and we belong to Christ, to whom be the glory and the power, together with the Father and the all-holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
